opening.headline: Learn how to allocate billing methods in a service that combines continuous, sudden spikes, and large-volume nighttime requests.
body: LLM service requests do not arrive in the same pattern throughout the day. There are steady requests during the day, sudden spikes during event times, and batch jobs running all at once in the early morning.

If we treat these patterns as a single billing method, one side may end up paying excessive costs or facing insufficient capacity. In this class, we will examine three types of traffic and follow examples of combining appropriate billing methods for each type.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the pricing combination by traffic type.
It can distinguish billing methods for continuous, sudden surge, and large-scale nighttime requests.
Can judge the cost efficiency of the combination

screens.title: When a single scaling method handles all traffic
screens.lead: Select each of the three segments one at a time from the graph illustrating daily request volume. An explanation will unfold on why a single billing method causes waste within each segment.

visual.alt: A graph showing request volume over a 24-hour period, displaying three segments: continuous, spike, and nighttime bulk.

items.prompt: Continuous interval: What would happen if we processed all daily requests by applying a volume-based limit only?
items.answer: During the day, a steady amount of usage typically flows in, making it possible to anticipate demand in advance. If, despite being able to anticipate usage, consumption is always charged at full price on a volumetric basis, the opportunity to reduce costs by pre-allocating capacity is lost.

items.prompt: Surge period: What happens if we pre-allocate capacity to handle the spike in requests during lunchtime or events?
items.answer: If capacity is purchased based on the peak demand, there will be excess capacity during normal times. Conversely, if capacity is purchased based on the average demand, there will be insufficient capacity during peak periods. The key challenge is how to balance the gap between average and peak demand.

items.prompt: Nighttime high-volume segment: What happens if we immediately process the work, which is accumulated and performed in the early morning, using an immediate response approach?
items.answer: This task does not need to respond immediately, as the results may appear hours later. Processing it in the same way as user requests would unnecessarily incur the cost of fast response times. For tasks that do not require immediacy, there are separate, cheaper, and slower processing methods available.

screens.outro: Since a problem was observed, now let us recall the shape of your service.

screens.title: What does the hourly traffic of our service look like?
screens.lead: First, think through each question in your mind. Do not enter or submit an answer. When you select a question, the instructor's thought summary will appear.

items.prompt: What is the difference in request volume between day and night on weekdays?
items.answer: If there is a significant difference between day and night, you can first estimate the volume of requests that consistently occur at a certain level throughout the day, i.e., the constant traffic volume. The minimum baseline that is maintained even during the least busy period becomes the standard for baseline traffic.

items.prompt: Do any sections experience sudden spikes in traffic during events or deadlines?
items.answer: If traffic spikes occur, that interval represents a surge in traffic. The frequency, duration, and magnitude—how many times higher than normal—determines the reservation capacity level.

items.prompt: Are there any tasks that don't need to be addressed immediately? For example, summarization, classification, or data augmentation tasks.
items.answer: This is a candidate for handling in bulk during off-peak hours. If a task does not require user responsiveness, you can reduce costs by sacrificing some response speed.

screens.outro: Based on these three forms, we will examine which types of funding mechanisms are appropriate for each category.

screens.title: Real-time, surge, nighttime bulk: matching funding solutions for three types
screens.lead: Select each tab to view features tailored to different traffic types and associated pricing options. After reviewing all three tabs, compare the differences.

tabs.label: Real-time traffic
tabs.body:
This is a steady request maintained at a certain level throughout the day. Since the volume can be predicted, it aligns well with the approach of pre-provisioning capacity.

Google's Provisioned Throughput reserves throughput at a fixed cost with a fixed-term subscription. The documentation targets use cases such as real-time chatbots or agents that require consistent, high throughput to deliver a consistent user experience and predictable costs.

OpenAI's Reserved Tier reserves a dollar amount per minute per model. This reserved capacity is added to the existing speed limits, and usage exceeding the reserved amount is billed at the standard pay-as-you-go rate.

tabs.label: Surge traffic
tabs.body:
Normally, demand is low but spikes suddenly at specific times. If reservations are scheduled to match the peak, the baseline capacity is increased; if reservations are set too low, demand may fall short during the peak.

Therefore, we consider a structure where reservations are set at or near the average level, and any excess beyond that is handled on a pay-as-you-go basis. OpenAI Reserved Tier aligns with this structure because users who exceed their reserved amount are automatically charged at the standard pay-as-you-go rate.

The key point is not to fully cover the spikes with reservations. Depending on how frequently spikes occur, handling the excess on a pay-as-you-go basis may be more efficient.

tabs.label: Nighttime bulk
tabs.body:
Tasks that do not require immediate responses. Activities such as summarization, classification, and data augmentation fall into this category, where results can be delivered at a later time.

OpenAI's cost-optimization documentation introduces the Batch API as an asynchronous processing method. It involves gathering requests into a single file to initiate a job, checking the job status, and then retrieving the results once completion is achieved. Flex processing, however, may result in slower response times and occasional resource wastage, albeit at lower costs.

Claude's pricing documentation states that the Batch API offers a 50% discount on both input and output tokens. This structure reduces the per-unit cost at the expense of immediate response times.

screens.outro: Since we've categorized the tools by type, let's look at the numbers to see how costs inside and outside of reservations are actually divided.

screens.title: Billing structure that varies depending on reservation amount
screens.lead: Move the slider to adjust the reserved amount per minute. You can compare how the reserved portion and the overage differ within the same 12-minute usage period.

visual.alt: A graph overlaying a bar chart showing per-minute usage volume for 12 minutes and a horizontal line indicating reserved amount.

stops.body: When the reserved amount is low, usage exceeds the reservation limit in nearly all of the 12 minutes. During this usage, approximately $11.8 is covered by the reservation, and about $9.3 is charged as overage. The overrun reservation charge is only about $0.2 from a 0.8-dollar minute. The overrun capacity is nearly zero, and since the reservation effectiveness is low, most usage is billed at the standard volumetric rate.

This is an example as described in the OpenAI documentation. For someone who spent $2.75, $2.00 is the reserved amount and $0.75 is the overage. Looking at the full 12-minute period, approximately $19.85 is reserved, with an overage of about $1.25. In contrast, for someone whose usage is less than $2.00, approximately $4.15 remains as reserved amount. This achieves a balanced and reasonable compromise between overage and overrun.

If the reserved amount is high, no surplus will be left for any individual. The full $21.1 for 12 minutes is entirely covered within the reserved portion. However, out of the reserved $36, approximately $14.9 remains unused and is effectively wasted. This option instead increases the usual available capacity by fully covering the peak demand, rather than strictly covering the peak. As a result, this usage pattern is less cost-efficient.

screens.outro: Now that we have acquired the sense of determining reservation size, let's follow an example of applying three methods together within a single service.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Reservation, Batch, On-Demand Combination Design
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the process of designing a combination by step-wise explaining with a service as an example. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Traffic View for Case Service
steps.body: The example is a customer inquiry chatbot. During regular hours, inquiries come in at a steady rate, but during weekly promotional events, the volume of inquiries increases several times over. At night, a batch process runs to summarize previous conversations and generate consultation records. Three different types of services are integrated within a single service.

steps.title: Step 1: Divide stage traffic into three groups
steps.body: First, we divide the requests into ongoing, spike, and nighttime bulk categories. For each category, we determine whether delay is acceptable. Delay is not acceptable for daytime inquiries and promotional inquiries, since users are waiting on-screen. However, delay is acceptable for early morning summaries, which only need to complete by morning.

steps.title: Step 2 continuous supply is covered by reservation.
steps.body: Low traffic queries have stable volume and responses are generated in front of the user. Such requests match the reserved capacity. By using mechanisms like Provisioned Throughput or Reserved Tier to pre-secure throughput, you achieve a consistent response experience and predictable costs.

steps.title: The third-stage surge is processed as a reservation adjusted to the average and as an overage under the rationing system.
steps.body: When booking according to the promotion tier, you get a large remaining capacity for the next 6 days. Therefore, reservations are set at normal levels, and any excess is delivered on-demand. In the Reserved Tier, usage exceeding the reserved amount is automatically charged at the standard pay-as-you-go rate, so no separate conversion is required.

steps.title: Step 4: Send night shift staff via assignment
steps.body: Early morning summary does not require immediacy. It is processed asynchronously via the Batch API. The Claude Batch API offers a 50% discount on both input and output tokens. One thing to note is that the Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex usage. Nightly jobs are calculated separately from reservations.

steps.title: Check the 5-step combination
steps.body: Finally, compare the monthly cost of the combination against the scenario where all requests are processed on-demand. Also verify how excess and underutilized capacity changes when reservation sizes are slightly increased and decreased. This comparison completes the design evaluation by confirming whether the combination is more advantageous than the single approach. The conclusion is simple: once traffic patterns are segmented, appropriate solutions naturally emerge for each segment.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the findings from the case study.

screens.title: Traffic patterns determine the billing combination.
screens.lead: Summarizes three types and their combination principle in one go. Read the following content and revisit the initial scene's problem.

paragraphs: The starting point of this course was the fact that three types of traffic—continuous, spike, and large-scale overnight—were mixed within a single service. If handled using a single approach, steady traffic would be charged at near-standard rates, spike traffic would lead to capacity shortages or excessive capacity allocation, and overnight traffic would be billed at unnecessary speeds.

The approach involves categorizing methods by type. Steady load is covered by reserved capacity, spike load keeps reservation near the average and spills excess through a volumetric mechanism, and nighttime bulk loads are sent using slower but cheaper methods such as batch or flex. The reserved amount is determined by balancing between the average and peak, considering the equilibrium between excess and idle capacity.

When evaluating cost efficiency, do not look at the reservation amount alone. Instead, compare the reservation volume, overbooked amounts, unused reservations, and batches and flex usage that are not applied together.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The pricing model is not selected first from the price list. Instead, we first analyze the traffic pattern and then tailor the pricing mechanism to match that pattern. If this order is reversed, inappropriate pricing models may be selected—therefore, please be cautious.

glossary.def: This is a steady stream of requests exceeding a certain threshold throughout the day. Since the volume can be predicted, it aligns well with reserved capacity.
A brief spike in requests at a specific time or event. The key issue is how to handle the difference between the average and the peak.
This task does not require immediate response and can be processed batch-wise, aligning well with approaches like Batch or Flex.
This is a pre-reserved capacity approach. In the OpenAI Reserved Tier, usage exceeding the reserved amount is billed at the standard pay-as-you-go rate.
This configuration mixes approaches such as reservation, metering, and scheduling according to traffic types.

misconceptions.myth: Once you book, all costs are reduced.
misconceptions.fact: Reservations are only efficient when consistently used. Unused reservations still incur costs, so setting them too high can lead to significant waste.

misconceptions.myth: Batch and Reserved Tier together result in overlapping discounts.
misconceptions.fact: According to the OpenAI documentation, the Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex usage. Large-scale overnight processing must be calculated separately from reservations.

misconceptions.myth: Choose one cheapest method, and that's it.
misconceptions.fact: The approach varies depending on traffic type. Uniformizing it into a single method would result in waste across all types, hence a combination is required.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Traffic patterns determine the billing combination.
Real-time is reserved, surge is over the reserved quota, and nighttime bulk is split into batches or flex.
The reserved amount is determined by balancing the excess over the average and the peak capacity.
The Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex usage, so overnight large-scale workloads are calculated separately.
closing.reflectionLead: This question is intended to encourage you to think through it on your own. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What mix of the three traffic types exists, and in what proportions do they combine to yield the best result?

title: Pricing combinations for different traffic types

checks.q: A user has a reservation of $2 per minute. One user's usage amount was $2.75. How is this user's bill calculated?
options: 2.75 dollars is charged in full as a volumetric fee.
The reservation fee of $2.00 is deducted, and only the excess of $0.75 is charged on a volumetric basis.
2.75 dollars is fully reserved with no additional charges.
Excess of 0.75 dollars is not charged and is carried forward to the next period.
checks.explain: Prepaid amounts are deducted based on the list price, and only the excess amount above the reservation is billed at the standard volumetric rate. Additional charges are not applied when actual usage is equal to or less than the reserved amount.

wrong.0: Reservations are first deducted, so not all are subject to volumetric billing.
wrong.2: Amounts exceeding the reservation amount are not covered by the reservation.
wrong.3: The explanation that excess amounts are carried over is not present in the document; instead, excess amounts are billed on a volumetric basis.
